title: Credit Scores
description: What a score weighs, and how to start one from nothing.
wolfLine: Your score is a rumor lenders believe. Pay on time and it stays kind.

credit-score.definition: A number that tells lenders how reliable you are at paying back money. Higher is better.
credit-score.example: A good score can get you a loan with a lower APR.

credit-limit.definition: The most you’re allowed to borrow on a credit card.
credit-limit.example: A card with a $2,000 limit lets you owe up to $2,000 on it.

credit-utilization.definition: How much of your credit limit you’re using, as a percentage: balance ├╖ limit. Lower is better for your credit score.
credit-utilization.example: Owe $500 on a $1,000 limit and your utilization is 50%.

hard-inquiry.definition: A credit check a lender makes when you apply to borrow. It can nudge your score down a little and stays on your report for about two years.
hard-inquiry.example: Applying for a car loan puts a hard inquiry on your report.

secured-card.definition: A credit card you qualify for by putting down a deposit, often equal to the limit. The deposit is the lender’s backup while you build a payment record.
secured-card.example: Put down $200, get a $200 limit, and use the card like any other.

credit-mix.definition: The variety of credit you have, such as a card and a loan. On a FICO score it is a small slice, about 10%.
credit-mix.example: One card and one car loan is a mix. Ten new cards is not the goal.

lessons.title: Credit Scores
lessons.summary: The reputation lenders check before they say yes.

steps.context: Your [[credit score]] is a number that tells lenders how reliable you are at paying back money. Higher is better.
steps.prompt: What does a high credit score usually get you?
choices: A higher salary
Easier approval and a lower APR
Free money from the bank
steps.explain: Lenders charge less to people they trust.

steps.prompt: Which habit helps your credit score most?
choices: Paying every bill on time
Opening lots of cards at once
Missing a payment now and then
steps.explain: On-time payments are the biggest single factor. Never miss.

steps.context: Your [[credit limit]] is the most you’re allowed to borrow on a card.
steps.prompt: Your card has a $5,000 credit limit. What does that mean?
choices: You must spend $5,000
You have $5,000 in savings
You can owe up to $5,000 on it
steps.explain: It’s a ceiling, not a target.

steps.context: [[Credit utilization]] is how much of your limit you’re using: balance ├╖ limit, as a percentage. Owe $500 on a $1,000 limit and you’re at 50%.
steps.prompt: Your limit is $5,000 and your balance is $1,500. What’s your utilization?
Lower credit utilization is generally better for your credit score.
steps.explain: Using a small slice of your limit shows you’re not stretched.

steps.prompt: Checking your own credit score lowers it.
steps.explain: Looking at your own score is free and harmless.

lessons.title: What the Score Weighs
lessons.summary: Five ingredients. Two of them do most of the work.

steps.title: FICO’s five factors
steps.body:
The FICO score, the one most lenders still use, weighs five things:

Payment history, about 35%. Amounts owed, about 30%. Length of history, about 15%. New credit, about 10%. [[Credit mix]], about 10%.

Other scores use their own recipes. These weights are FICO’s, and they are the ones to remember.

steps.prompt: On a FICO score, which factor weighs the most?
choices: Payment history, about 35%
Credit mix, about 10%
New credit, about 10%
steps.explain: On-time payments are the biggest slice.

steps.prompt: Which factor is about 30%?
choices: Amounts owed
Length of history
Credit mix
steps.explain: How much of your limits you are using lives here.

steps.prompt: Match the FICO factor to its weight.
Every credit score in the country uses these exact five weights.
steps.explain: FICO does. Other scores have their own formulas.

steps.prompt: You can control which two factors fastest?
choices: Paying on time, and keeping balances low
The year you opened your first card
How many cards you have ever opened
steps.explain: History length takes years. Payments and balances move now.

lessons.title: Payment History
lessons.summary: One late payment echoes. A long streak of on-time ones helps.

steps.context: Your [[credit score]] cares most about whether you pay on time. A paid-off bill and a [[minimum payment]] made by the [[due date]] both count as on time. Late is late.
steps.prompt: What helps a credit score the most, month after month?
choices: Paying every bill on time
Carrying a balance so the card “sees activity”
Opening a new card each month
steps.explain: Payment history is the heaviest factor.

steps.prompt: Paying only the minimum, but paying it by the due date, still counts as on time.
steps.explain: On time and “paid in full” are different jobs. The score is watching the due date.

steps.prompt: A payment is 30 days late. What is the likely effect?
choices: It can hurt the score and stay on the report for years
Nothing, if you pay the next day
The score goes up, because you used the card
steps.explain: Thirty days late is a negative mark. Under federal rules it can stay about seven years.

steps.prompt: You have 24 months of payments and 1 of them was late. How many were on time?
steps.explain: 24 − 1 = 23. One miss still stings.

steps.prompt: Which is the safer habit?
choices: Autopay at least the minimum, then pay extra when you can
Paying in full, whenever you remember
Paying a day after the due date to earn interest
steps.explain: Autopay covers the “on time” job. Extra payments do the “get out of debt” job.

steps.prompt: A single late payment is a secret. Lenders never see it.
steps.explain: It can land on your credit report.

lessons.title: Utilization Math
lessons.summary: Read three cards, then work out what the score sees.

steps.context: [[Credit utilization]] is balance ÷ [[credit limit]]. Scores look at each card and at all of them together. A common rule of thumb is to stay under 30%, and lower is better.
steps.prompt: What is the utilization on the Harbor Card alone?
And on the City Store Card?
Add up the three limits. What is your total credit limit?
What is your overall utilization: total balance ÷ total limit?
You have $300 extra this month. Where does it fix the worst number?
choices: Pay down the City Store Card
Pay down the Cloud Card
Split it evenly across all three
why: That card is already at 7.5%. The store card is the one at 80%.
Helpful, but the store card stays high.
steps.explain: $100 left on a $500 limit is 20%, down from 80%.

steps.prompt: Maxing out a card, even if you pay on time, can still hurt the score.
steps.explain: On-time payments and high utilization are different factors.

lessons.title: Nina’s Oldest Card
lessons.summary: Old accounts are a track record. Closing one can cost more than the fee.

story.title: The old student card
story.body:
Nina opened her first credit card at **21**: a student card with a **$1,000** limit. She has used it for gas ever since and paid it in full every month. Two years ago she added a second card with a **$3,000** limit.

Now the student card charges a **$45** annual fee, and she is thinking of closing it. Her statements usually add up to about **$800** across both cards, which she pays in full.

steps.context: Length of history is about 15% of a FICO score. An old card you keep open and pay can help. Closing your oldest card can shorten the story lenders see.
steps.prompt: What does “length of credit history” look at?
choices: How long your accounts have been open
How long you have had your current job
How long until your loans are paid off
steps.explain: Older, well-kept accounts help.

steps.prompt: Nina is 29 and opened the student card at 21. How old is that account?
Closing the student card could shorten the history lenders see.
steps.explain: It is her oldest account.

steps.prompt: With both cards open, her $800 is what share of her $4,000 total limit?
If she closes the $1,000 card, what share of the remaining $3,000 limit is $800? Round to the nearest whole percent.
steps.explain: $800 ÷ $3,000 = 0.267, about 27%. Same spending, higher utilization.

steps.prompt: What is a common middle path for Nina?
choices: Ask the issuer to switch it to a no-fee card and keep it open
Close it and open a new card to replace the limit
Close it, since old accounts stop counting after five years
why: A new card means a hard inquiry and a brand-new account.
Old accounts keep counting. That’s the point of this factor.
steps.explain: She keeps the history and the limit, and drops the fee.

lessons.title: New Credit and Hard Inquiries
lessons.summary: Shopping for a loan leaves footprints. Checking yourself does not.

steps.context: A [[hard inquiry]] happens when you apply for credit. It can dip a score a little and stays on the report for about two years. You checking your own score is not a hard inquiry.
steps.prompt: What is a hard inquiry?
choices: A lender checking your credit because you applied to borrow
You looking at your own score
A store mailing you an ad
steps.explain: You asked to borrow, so they looked.

steps.prompt: Looking up your own credit score lowers it.
steps.explain: That check is yours. It does not count as a hard inquiry.

steps.prompt: You apply for four cards in one week. What is the likely result?
choices: Several hard inquiries, and maybe a lower score
A higher score, because you have more credit available
The old inquiries get deleted
steps.explain: A burst of new applications looks risky.

steps.prompt: Rate-shopping one car loan at three lenders in a short window is often treated more kindly than four random cards. Why?
choices: Scoring models often group loan shopping into one search
Car loans don’t appear on credit reports
Lenders delete inquiries once a loan is approved
steps.explain: One car, one search. Do not stretch it across months.

steps.prompt: A hard inquiry stays about two years. You applied in 2026. About what year does it drop off?
A lender’s credit check when you apply is a ___ inquiry.
choices: hard
soft
monthly
steps.explain: Hard inquiry. Your own check is the harmless kind.

lessons.title: Score Myths
lessons.summary: Sort the rumor from the rule.

steps.context: The score measures how you handle borrowed money, not how big your paycheck is.
steps.prompt: Myth or fact?
items: Carrying a balance on purpose raises your score
Checking your own score lowers it
You must earn a high income to have a high score
Paying on time is the heaviest FICO factor
High utilization can hurt even when you pay on time
A hard inquiry can nudge a score down

steps.prompt: You pay the statement in full every month. Are you “failing” to build credit?
choices: No. On-time, paid-in-full use is a strong record
Yes. You must leave a balance
Yes. Interest is what builds the score
steps.explain: Interest is a cost, not a strategy.

steps.prompt: A higher income automatically means a higher credit score.
steps.explain: Income is not a FICO factor.

steps.prompt: Someone says “close all your cards so you have zero debt and a perfect score.” What is wrong?
choices: Closing cards can shorten history and raise utilization on what remains
Nothing. Zero cards is the top score
Cards cannot be closed
steps.explain: Zero debt is good. Zero history is a blank page.

steps.prompt: Two cards, $1,000 limit each. You close one. You still owe $400. What is utilization now?
Which statement is a fact?
choices: Lower utilization is generally better
Maxing out a card helps the mix factor
Late payments vanish after one month
steps.explain: Keep the slice you use small.
